opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the motivation behind something like EnigmaEval is that a lot of our existing benchmarks have become quite saturated, and many of them test fairly short-horizon skills. You ask a question, there's a crisp answer, and the model either knows the fact or can do a few steps of reasoning to get there. That's useful, but it doesn't really capture what intellectual work looks like when people actually do it.

Puzzle-hunt style problems are interesting because they're unstructured. You're not told what the task is. You get a pile of text, images, maybe some strange grid, and you have to figure out what's even being asked before you can solve it. That's much closer to research or real problem-solving, where most of the difficulty is in framing the problem, generating hypotheses, noticing that some pattern is a red herring, backtracking, and stitching together multiple insights across modalities.

So it stresses a few things at once. There's lateral thinking: you need creative leaps, not just grinding through a known procedure. There's long chains of dependent reasoning, where if you get one step wrong, everything downstream falls apart, so error accumulation really matters. And there's verification. A lot of these puzzles have a satisfying "click" when you're right, and a good solver uses that to check their work. Models are often bad at knowing when they've actually solved something versus confabulating a plausible-looking answer.

That said, I wouldn't claim any single benchmark fully captures longer-horizon work. Puzzles are still bounded. They're designed to have one intended answer and to be solvable by humans in hours or days. Real intellectual work, like running a research agenda, involves open-endedness, managing resources, deciding which questions are even worth pursuing, and operating over weeks or months. So I think of it as one piece of a portfolio. It tells you something about flexible, multi-step, creative reasoning that multiple-choice exams don't, and when models score very low on it while acing graduate-level exams, that gap is informative. It suggests there's a difference between having a lot of crystallized knowledge and having the fluid, exploratory reasoning you'd need to automate a lot of cognitive labor.

And from a safety and forecasting standpoint, that's exactly what we want to track. If these kinds of evaluations start getting solved, that's a meaningful signal that we're getting closer to systems that can do autonomous intellectual work, which has big implications for things like automated AI research.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that it captures it only partially, and we should be clear-eyed about that. What Enigma does well is move beyond the "answer in one shot" regime that most benchmarks live in. Instead of a question with a crisp answer you can grade in ten seconds, you're looking at tasks where the model has to hold a problem in mind across many steps, form hypotheses, discard the ones that don't work, and keep track of what it's already learned. That's much closer to what a researcher or an analyst actually does over a day or a week than something like a multiple-choice exam.

But I'd push back on the idea that any evaluation like this fully captures long-horizon intellectual work. The hard parts of real research are often the parts that don't fit neatly into a task format. Knowing which problem is worth working on. Noticing that the framing you started with is wrong. Being willing to throw away a month of effort. Those are judgment calls, and they're very difficult to score. When you build a benchmark, you inevitably compress all of that into something with a defined endpoint and a defined success criterion, and some of the richness gets lost in that compression.

The other thing I'd flag is that longer horizons amplify small errors. If a model has a one percent chance of making a critical mistake at each step, then over a hundred steps that compounds into a system that's unreliable most of the time. So evaluations like Enigma are really measuring something like consistency and recovery, not just raw intelligence. A model that's brilliant for five steps and then goes off the rails is going to look bad, and I think that's the right thing to be measuring, because that's exactly the failure mode that matters when you're deploying these systems on real work.

Where I'd like to see this go is toward evaluations that are harder to saturate and that track capability over time rather than giving us a single number that gets maxed out in eighteen months. The point of a benchmark isn't to say "we're done." It's to give us a sense of where the frontier is and how fast it's moving, so we can make decisions about safety and governance that are grounded in evidence instead of intuition.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between something that’s difficult because you need one clever insight and something that’s difficult because you have to sustain a coherent process over many steps. Those aren’t the same capability. You can be very good at answering a hard question in a few minutes and still struggle with work that requires planning, checking intermediate results, and revising your approach.

So the question I’d ask about Enigma is whether the tasks actually require that sustained process. Does an early mistake create problems later? Do you have to notice that you’re stuck and change strategies? And does giving the model more time translate into meaningful progress, rather than just a longer answer?

I wouldn’t equate performance on an evaluation with being able to carry out an entire research project. In research, you also have to decide which questions are worth pursuing, and often what would even count as success. But evaluating whether a model can reliably carry a difficult task through to completion is an important part of that picture.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between a question that requires a clever insight and a task that requires sustained intellectual work. A lot of evaluations focus on the first: can you recognize the trick, apply the right technique, and produce an answer? But longer-horizon work involves trying an approach, discovering that it doesn’t work, revising your assumptions, and keeping track of what you’ve learned.

The way I think about Enigma is that it pushes toward that second kind of evaluation. You want problems where making progress requires a sequence of decisions, and where an early mistake can send you down an unproductive path. That tests whether the model can recover and use additional time effectively, rather than just generate a longer response.

Of course, that still captures only part of intellectual work. In research, choosing the problem and deciding what constitutes a useful result are themselves difficult. So I’d view it as a step toward measuring sustained problem-solving, rather than a complete measure of someone’s ability to do research.
